paragraphs: Generalized Bayesian inference can adjust how strongly observations influence an inference, helping address overconfidence when a model does not fully match reality. Existing methods often repeat expensive sampling for every new dataset and temperature setting. This paper targets the specific posterior family formed by raising the likelihood to a positive power, beta, and combining it with the prior.

The authors train one neural posterior estimator that takes both observations and beta as inputs. Once trained, it produces samples in a single forward pass without further simulator calls or inference-time MCMC. They offer two training routes: generating samples for the tempered setting, or reweighting an existing dataset using self-normalized importance sampling.

For the reweighting route, the authors establish a consistent forward-KL fitting objective under finite importance-weight variance. Across four simulation-based inference benchmarks, including Lorenz–96, the estimator produces posterior approximations competitive with non-amortized MCMC methods across a wide temperature range. The contribution is reusable inference across datasets and temperatures within this particular posterior family.
icml-2026-amortized-simulation-based-inf.tldr: A single neural estimator learns tempered Bayesian posteriors across observations and temperatures, enabling sampling without inference-time simulation or MCMC.

paragraphs: Graph foundation models seek to learn reusable knowledge during pretraining, but it remains unclear which graph structures transfer between tasks. This paper approaches that question through the functional behavior of substructures. Its theoretical contribution connects transferable substructures to the intrinsic geometry of the space in which the model represents graphs.

To learn that geometry, the authors introduce Geometric Morphology Learning. The framework works with local coordinates organized in a neural vector bundle, providing a way to describe local representation geometry. Their architecture, Gauge, constructs this bundle and flattens local coordinates when they are geometrically compatible. A new Dirichlet loss supports the framework and also measures transfer effort.

This approach gives structural transfer a geometric basis beyond identifying recurring discrete patterns. The authors evaluate Gauge on challenging tasks that include zero-shot link prediction and graph isomorphism, reporting superior expressive ability. These findings support the usefulness of the proposed geometric representations for the evaluated tasks, alongside the paper’s theoretical account of how substructures can transfer.
icml-2026-are-common-substructures-trans.tldr: Gauge connects graph-substructure transfer to representation geometry and learns that geometry through neural vector bundles.

paragraphs: Vehicles can share observations to support decisions when their individual views are obstructed. Multimodal language models make language-based reasoning possible in this setting, but densely exchanging and combining visual tokens creates communication and inference costs. The paper addresses how to reduce those tokens while accounting for both the question being answered and overlap between vehicles’ observations.

V2V-CCM uses a two-stage communication framework that broadcasts request messages to participating agents. Its Question Semantic Message represents the overall intent of the question, helping select relevant tokens. Its Spatial Coverage Message summarizes LiDAR features so the system can identify spatial information that other agents have already observed.

These two messages provide complementary selection criteria: relevance to the question and redundancy across viewpoints. The authors report substantial reductions in communication and inference costs while preserving question-relevant information. On V2V-QA and V2V-GoT-QA, the framework consistently outperforms existing pruning methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance. The results support coordinating token selection around the cooperative task and shared spatial coverage.
icml-2026-ask-less-see-more-communicatio.tldr: V2V-CCM uses question intent and shared LiDAR coverage to reduce communication and inference costs in cooperative vehicle reasoning.

paragraphs: Computer-aided design commonly describes objects through boundary representations, which encode their surfaces and curves precisely. Learning from these representations presents a tension: continuous descriptions preserve analytical geometry but are visually abstract, while discrete descriptions are easier to interpret spatially but sacrifice precision. Brep2Shape aims to connect abstract boundary information with the shapes it describes.

The framework uses self-supervised pretraining to predict dense spatial points from parametric Bézier control points. This task trains the model to relate geometric coefficients to their resulting physical shape. A dual transformer processes surface tokens and curve tokens in separate streams, allowing each stream to capture the properties of its own geometric elements.

Topology attention then models relationships between surfaces and curves to maintain consistency in how those elements connect. Together, these components align geometric meaning with both the parameters and structure of a CAD representation. The authors report scalability, state-of-the-art accuracy, and faster convergence across multiple downstream tasks, supporting the value of this alignment as a pretraining objective.
icml-2026-brep2shape-boundary-and-shape-.tldr: Brep2Shape learns to connect precise CAD boundary parameters with spatial shape through self-supervised prediction and geometry-aware transformers.

paragraphs: People can know what they want without being able to express it completely in an instruction. This paper treats that gap as a collaboration problem: an agent should ask questions that resolve uncertainty about the user’s intent. The proposed agent, Nous, learns a questioning policy intended to reduce inefficient cycles of attempted instructions and unsatisfactory outputs.

Its training reward measures the information gained through dialogue. Within a structured task space, this gain corresponds to a reduction in Shannon entropy, a measure of uncertainty. That gives the agent an intrinsic signal for learning useful inquiry without requiring costly human preference annotations or an external reward model.

The authors develop an automated simulation pipeline that creates a large preference-based dataset for scientific diagram generation. They assess the framework through ablations, subjective and objective evaluations, and tests involving different levels of user expertise. The reported findings show leading efficiency and output quality, with robustness across expertise levels. The work supports training clarification as an explicit capability for complex tasks with ambiguous intentions.
icml-2026-closing-the-expression-gap-in-.tldr: Nous learns to ask clarifying questions using information gain as a reward, improving scientific diagram collaboration across user expertise levels.

paragraphs: E-commerce disputes require identifying decisive clues within repetitive evidence collected across multiple rounds and formats. Decisions also depend on flexible platform conventions, making this setting different from formal legal judgment. The paper introduces E-commerce Dispute Verdicts as a task and VerdictBench, a multimodal benchmark containing 6,000 real cases that reflect crowdsourced jury decisions.

CyberJurors organizes reasoning at both the individual and group levels. Each simulated juror follows four structured reasoning stages to examine clues and connect them causally to the central dispute. The collective process then uses multiple rounds of discussion and voting, incorporating verdict precedents to reduce bias toward either side.

The design combines detailed evidence interpretation with a regulated consensus process. On VerdictBench, CyberJurors outperforms state-of-the-art language models, multimodal language models, and court simulators. Its outputs also align more closely with real jury voting patterns. These results show that a framework tailored to platform disputes can better reproduce the benchmark’s crowdsourced decision process.
icml-2026-cyberjurors-a-multi-agent-simu.tldr: CyberJurors combines structured individual reasoning with discussion and voting to improve e-commerce dispute verdicts on a 6,000-case benchmark.

paragraphs: Compositional diffusion planners try to build long robot plans from short training trajectories. Existing methods often join local predictions through heuristic stitching. The paper shows that the combined update generally fails to correspond to any valid probability density over complete trajectories: its correction field is non-conservative, meaning the local updates do not derive from one global scalar objective.

Energy-based Compositional Diffuser addresses this by defining a global trajectory through the sum of local bridge potentials. Minimizing that energy provides a consistent global objective and produces a conservative correction field. The formulation also reveals a boundary reaction term that heuristic stitching leaves out.

For efficient inference, the authors approximate the score using a Markov-based construction. This computes the reaction term with one block-tridiagonal solve, keeping time complexity linear in the planning horizon. On OGBench stitching tasks, ECD achieves state-of-the-art success rates while nearly matching heuristic methods’ inference speed. The results suggest that a mathematically consistent composition rule can improve planning without a large speed penalty.
icml-2026-energy-based-compositional-dif.tldr: ECD replaces heuristic trajectory stitching with a global energy formulation, improving planning success while nearly preserving stitching speed.

paragraphs: Answering questions with a knowledge base requires translating ordinary language into executable queries that respect the database’s schema. A plausible-looking query can fail if it refers to nonexistent schema elements. The paper also identifies a different problem: models can copy rigid reasoning templates without adequately responding to the knowledge base they are actually using.

KBQA-R1 trains the model through reinforcement learning in a multi-turn decision process. A structured set of actions lets it navigate the knowledge base, and execution feedback informs its reasoning strategy. This makes interaction with the environment part of learning how to answer, rather than relying solely on imitation of prewritten traces.

To initialize this process, Referenced Rejection Sampling generates training data whose reasoning traces strictly follow ground-truth action sequences. This addresses the cold-start problem before interaction-based optimization. Experiments on WebQSP, GrailQA, and GraphQuestions report state-of-the-art performance. The findings support combining carefully aligned initial traces with feedback from actual execution to improve knowledge-base question answering.
icml-2026-kbqa-r1-reinforcing-large-lang.tldr: KBQA-R1 learns to answer knowledge-base questions through structured interactions and execution feedback, achieving state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts language models route inputs to selected expert modules, increasing model capacity while controlling computation. This paper identifies a vulnerability called Safety Sparsity: safety capabilities can become concentrated in only a few experts, leaving opportunities for adversarial bypass. It also argues that uniformly adapting all parameters can interfere with the different functions those parameters serve.

MESA distributes safety responsibility more deliberately. Using optimal transport theory, its Expert Capacity Reallocation mechanism assigns safety duties to experts according to a transport cost matrix. The aim is to expand safety coverage through cost-effective assignments while limiting disruption to useful capabilities. Dynamic Routing Refinement then constrains the router to activate the appropriate decentralized safety modules.

The two mechanisms address both where safety capabilities reside and whether inputs reach them. Experiments report robust defensive performance across varied harmful benchmarks while maintaining helpfulness. These findings support alignment that accounts for expert specialization and routing behavior, rather than treating an MoE model as a uniform collection of parameters.
icml-2026-mesa-improving-moe-safety-alig.tldr: MESA spreads safety capabilities across selected MoE experts and refines routing to improve defenses while preserving helpfulness.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can pose a privacy risk by connecting scattered information about a person, even when no single input contains a complete profile. This paper distinguishes detecting private information from reasoning across fragments to infer personal attributes and identities. It argues that existing privacy benchmarks focus too heavily on detection to capture this broader capability.

MultiPriv evaluates that capability through the Privacy Perception and Reasoning framework. Its bilingual multimodal dataset uses synthetic individual profiles that connect identifiers, including faces and names, with sensitive attributes. Nine tasks cover attribute detection, recognizing the same individual across images, and chained inference from distributed information.

The authors evaluate more than 50 open-source and commercial vision-language models. In this controlled benchmark, 60% of widely used models demonstrate individual-level privacy reasoning, with accuracy reaching up to 80%. Those figures describe performance on the constructed tasks. They indicate a potential privacy threat from linking multimodal evidence and motivate evaluating inference capabilities alongside straightforward recognition of sensitive content.
icml-2026-multipriv-benchmarking-individ.tldr: MultiPriv tests whether vision-language models can link scattered multimodal clues into individual profiles, revealing substantial capability in a controlled synthetic benchmark.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks promise efficient inference, but short simulations often leave them less accurate than conventional neural networks on images. Under matched architectures and budgets, this paper finds a consistently smaller accuracy gap on representative continuous one-dimensional signal benchmarks. The authors attribute the difference to how naturally spiking neurons accumulate evidence arriving over time.

Static images typically require conversion from amplitudes to spikes, which introduces estimation error over short windows. Guided by this explanation, the authors combine two encoding methods. Multi-Scale Temporal Encoding supplies streams at different temporal scales and uses scale-aligned, multi-bit integer spikes to carry more information per step. Sparsity-Regularized Transform Encoding replaces a controllable fraction of leaky integrate-and-fire units with transform-encoding neurons.

The transform neurons use auxiliary reconstruction and sparsity objectives, with their synthesis branch needed only during training. Across varied one-dimensional datasets and backbone families, the combined framework improves the accuracy-efficiency balance over standard spiking baselines. It matches or sometimes exceeds conventional counterparts, supporting temporal signals as a favorable setting for these designs.
icml-2026-narrowing-the-annsnn-gap-for-c.tldr: Multi-scale and sparsity-regularized encoding improve spiking networks’ accuracy-efficiency trade-off for continuous temporal signals, sometimes surpassing conventional counterparts.

paragraphs: Foundation models for partial differential equations aim to reuse learned knowledge across different physical systems. A central challenge is separating the varied dynamics in pretraining data into elementary patterns that generalize. Another is explaining which learned components actually help solve a new equation. Origo addresses these linked problems of transfer and interpretability.

The paper introduces neural operator splitting, which decomposes PDE evolution into a modulated global spectral operator and sparse local constitutive mechanisms. This separates a global component of the dynamics from local mechanisms. Origo organizes learned operators into a bank, providing a basis for identifying generalization patterns at the operator level.

The significance of this organization is that transfer can be examined in terms of the model’s constituent mechanisms. The authors report strong zero-shot generalization on unseen PDEs, together with mechanism-level interpretability. Their experiments support using the proposed decomposition to learn across different physics while making the transferred operator knowledge more understandable.
icml-2026-origo-interpretable-multi-phys.tldr: Origo decomposes PDE dynamics into reusable global and local operators, supporting zero-shot transfer and interpretable generalization to unseen equations.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation can fail even when useful evidence is present among retrieved passages. This paper argues that relevance alone does not determine whether evidence suits the generator. Some passages reveal the answer too directly to provide a strong learning signal, while others omit information needed to answer at all.

BAR-RAG trains a selector to target evidence that is challenging but still sufficient for the generator to reason from. The selector learns through reinforcement learning using feedback from the generator. A two-stage pipeline also fine-tunes the generator on the evidence distribution produced by selection, reducing the mismatch between its training inputs and what it encounters during inference.

The approach therefore coordinates evidence selection with the capabilities and learning needs of the answering model. On knowledge-intensive question-answering benchmarks with noisy retrieval, BAR-RAG consistently improves end-to-end performance. The authors report an average gain of 10.3% over strong retrieval-augmented generation and reranking baselines, alongside substantially improved robustness. The findings support treating evidence suitability as more than topical relevance.
icml-2026-rethinking-the-reranker-bounda.tldr: BAR-RAG selects challenging but sufficient evidence using generator feedback, improving question answering and robustness under noisy retrieval.

paragraphs: Model editing changes a language model’s stored information without retraining the entire model. This paper examines a privacy vulnerability in locate-then-edit methods: the parameter changes can themselves reveal information about the edited data. The concern is a side channel in the update, separate from what the edited model says in ordinary responses.

The proposed KSTER attack has two stages and exploits the low-rank structure of parameter updates. The authors theoretically show that an update matrix’s row space contains a fingerprint of the edited subjects, which supports subject recovery through spectral analysis. An entropy-based prompt recovery stage then reconstructs the semantic context associated with the edit.

Experiments across multiple language models report high success rates in recovering edited data. The authors also propose subspace camouflage, which obscures the fingerprint using semantic decoys. They report that this defense reduces reconstruction risk without compromising editing utility. The work shows why evaluating an editing method’s privacy requires considering information exposed by its parameter updates as well as its resulting behavior.
icml-2026-reverse-engineering-model-edit.tldr: KSTER recovers edited information from model-update structure, while a proposed camouflage defense reduces this leakage without harming editing utility.

paragraphs: Model merging combines knowledge from separately fine-tuned models without training a new model from scratch. Many methods manipulate the weight differences created by fine-tuning. This paper instead examines which parts of the original pretrained weights support generalization, asking whether preserving particular parameter directions can improve the merged result.

The authors define a core subspace using dominant singular vectors. They find that pretrained weight components in this subspace are essential to generalization across diverse tasks. Empirically, the multi-task loss has nearly zero first-order change and predominantly non-negative curvature there, indicating near-optimality within that subspace. This evidence motivates placing task-specific changes mainly in its orthogonal complement.

The resulting strategy preserves the core pretrained components while incorporating adaptations in complementary directions. Experiments on vision and vision-language tasks consistently improve on training-free merging methods including Task Arithmetic, LOT Merging, ISO, and TSV. The findings support a subspace-aware merging strategy; the near-optimality evidence concerns the identified core subspace rather than a claim of global optimality.
icml-2026-revisiting-the-role-of-pretrai.tldr: Preserving a core subspace of pretrained weights while merging adaptations into complementary directions improves training-free model merging.

paragraphs: Medical classification can draw on sources such as images and clinical text, but many fusion methods assume a fixed set of input modalities. This paper proposes a framework designed to accommodate an arbitrary number of modalities. Its central idea is to make the sources agree about shared meaning at both broad and detailed levels.

At the modality level, each source represents its estimate of latent semantics as a probability distribution that accounts for uncertainty. Symmetric consistency constraints align those estimates across sources. At the token level, a linear reconstruction constraint enables local pieces of information from different modalities to verify one another in a structured way.

For the final prediction, the framework treats each modality in turn as a conditional view, using it to suppress noise in the others and extract shared semantics. These views contribute to a unified representation for diagnosis prediction. Experiments on five public and self-constructed medical datasets demonstrate effectiveness and scalability, supporting consistency modeling as a way to combine changing collections of medical inputs.
icml-2026-scalable-medical-multimodal-fu.tldr: A modality-agnostic fusion framework aligns uncertain global meanings and local details to combine varying numbers of medical data sources.

paragraphs: Long tasks can overwhelm a language-model agent’s context with intermediate actions and observations. Existing frameworks often handle this through manually designed context-management procedures. Context Folding gives the agent an explicit way to manage its own working context as part of carrying out the task.

The agent can branch into a separate sub-trajectory for a subtask. After completing that work, it folds the branch: intermediate steps are collapsed, while a concise summary of the outcome remains available. FoldGRPO trains this behavior end to end with reinforcement learning. Its process rewards encourage useful task decomposition and effective context management, making the decisions about branching and folding learnable.

On long-horizon tasks, the resulting agent matches baseline performance while using an active context up to ten times smaller. It also significantly outperforms models given the same context-size constraint. These findings indicate that learned management of intermediate work can make limited active context more useful, while the reported context reduction specifically concerns what remains in the agent’s working context.
icml-2026-scaling-long-horizon-agent-via.tldr: Context Folding trains agents to summarize completed subtask branches, matching baseline performance with active context up to ten times smaller.

paragraphs: Computer-use agents built from vision-language models often depend on human-labeled examples and struggle with unfamiliar specialized software. SEAgent addresses learning in those environments through direct experience. Agents explore software, learn through trial and error, and work through automatically generated tasks that progress from simple to more demanding.

A World State Model assesses trajectories step by step, while a Curriculum Generator supplies increasingly varied and challenging tasks. Policy updates combine adversarial imitation of failure actions with Group Relative Policy Optimization on successful actions. These components organize experience into feedback and progressively harder practice, rather than requiring human annotations for each new software setting.

The framework also combines what specialist agents learn into a generalist agent. The authors report that this unified agent surpasses ensembles of individual specialists on their specialized software. Evaluations cover five professional software environments across OSWorld, ScienceBoard, and AndroidWorld, with a significant improvement over UI-TARS. The results support experiential adaptation and consolidation of software-specific learning into broader computer-use capability.
icml-2026-seagent-self-evolving-computer.tldr: SEAgent improves computer-use agents through autonomous software exploration, generated curricula, and consolidation of specialist experience into a generalist.

paragraphs: Visual spatial reasoning has advanced in indoor scenes, but extending it across different physical scales requires broader data and modeling. SpaceVista addresses reliance on indoor scans and costly annotations, alongside models’ tendency to specialize in single-scene settings. It combines a structured spatial knowledge system, scale-aware modeling, and progressive training.

An automated pipeline driven by task-specific specialist models collects more than 38,000 video scenes across five spatial scales. The resulting SpaceVista-1M dataset contains one million spatial questions and answers across 19 tasks. Because the specialists are unreliable evaluators, the authors separately build a precisely annotated benchmark through manual video recording and retrieval.

The paper reports that simply training on the combined dataset can be suboptimal because of potential knowledge conflicts. SpaceVista-7B therefore uses scale to organize specialized experts and progressive rewards, with inputs extending beyond semantics. Evaluations across five benchmarks show competitive performance and generalization across scales and scenarios. The contribution joins broader coverage with a model designed to account for differences between scales.
icml-2026-spacevista-all-scale-visual-sp.tldr: SpaceVista combines a million-question dataset with scale-aware training to extend visual spatial reasoning across five physical scales.

paragraphs: Diffusion inversion maps an image back into a diffusion model’s Gaussian latent space, supporting reconstruction and editing. Fast deterministic inversion with DDIM introduces deviations that can accumulate into visible errors. This paper examines an overlooked source of those errors: the choice of timesteps in the noise schedule.

The authors find that inversion deviation depends strongly on timestep size and follows a parabolic trend, with larger errors at both small and large timesteps. They use this observation to design a nonuniform schedule. Global rescaling and local rescheduling through dynamic programming allocate computational effort more strategically to reduce overall inversion error.

The scheduler is designed as an enhancement to existing inversion techniques, requiring no additional parameters or computational overhead. Experiments show consistent improvements when it is integrated into existing methods, with better reconstruction and editing results. The contribution is a way to improve the accuracy of the inversion process by reconsidering where its steps occur, making timestep selection an explicit part of controlling accumulated error.
icml-2026-timestep-rescheduling-in-diffu.tldr: A nonuniform timestep scheduler reduces diffusion-inversion errors and improves reconstruction and editing without added parameters or computational overhead.

paragraphs: Offline black-box optimization seeks better designs using an existing dataset of designs and their labels, often with few labeled examples. The paper argues that left-to-right language generation struggles with design problems whose parts depend strongly on one another in both directions. It adapts diffusion language models to take advantage of their bidirectional modeling.

A central challenge is the mismatch between natural-language pretraining and the mixture of prompts, designs, and labels used in optimization. The authors build a unified prompt-response corpus and add delimiter tokens to mark field boundaries. This gives the model an explicit structure for distinguishing the different kinds of information during adaptation.

Training then proceeds in two stages. Supervised fine-tuning teaches masked-response prediction on the unified data, and reinforcement learning rewards improvements in design labels. The authors report state-of-the-art results on Design-Bench under small-data conditions. The findings support combining bidirectional generation with domain-specific formatting and reward-based refinement to search for improved designs from limited offline examples.
icml-2026-training-diffusion-language-mo.tldr: Diffusion language models adapted with structured data and two-stage training achieve state-of-the-art small-data optimization results on Design-Bench.

paragraphs: Robots learning manipulation from limited demonstrations can reach unfamiliar states where their learned world models predict poorly. Sparse rewards make successful behavior difficult to discover. In multi-stage tasks, updating a learned reward function alongside the policy also creates a moving target, increasing the effect of uncertainty on learning.

QUEST is a model-based reinforcement learning framework that uses uncertainty to adjust the balance between exploration and exploitation. Intrinsic rewards encourage exploration, while an ensemble of dynamics models supports uncertainty-guided planning. A hybrid sampling strategy gives priority to rare successful transitions between task stages, making those valuable experiences more prominent during learning.

On challenging sparse-reward manipulation tasks with limited expert demonstrations, the authors report improvements over state-of-the-art methods averaging 17%, with gains reaching 60% on difficult tasks. They also demonstrate zero-shot transfer from simulation to five real-world tasks. These findings support coordinating exploration, planning, and experience sampling around uncertainty and scarce successful transitions in the evaluated manipulation settings.
icml-2026-uncertainty-guided-exploration.tldr: QUEST uses uncertainty-guided planning and prioritized successful transitions to improve sparse-reward robot learning from limited demonstrations.

paragraphs: Boolean satisfiability problems involve clauses built from positive and negative literals. Learning useful representations requires capturing both interactions among clauses and the complementary relationship between the two forms of a variable. This paper targets unsat-core prediction, arguing that common graph representations capture these higher-order and polarity-related properties less directly.

The proposed framework represents formulas as clause-literal hypergraphs, supplemented by a clause incidence graph. This structure models interactions involving groups of literals and clauses. A polarity-aware decomposition separates each variable’s representation into an invariant component and an equivariant component, allowing the model to represent both shared information and information that changes with polarity.

The resulting literal representations propagate through the hypergraph. During training, polarity-inversion consistency regularization further encourages representations to behave consistently when polarity is inverted. Experiments on multiple SAT datasets demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness. The contribution combines a representation of clause-level structure with an explicit treatment of positive-negative relationships, giving the learning system access to two important aspects of SAT formulas.
icml-2026-unsat-core-prediction-through-.tldr: A polarity-aware hypergraph framework improves SAT representation learning by explicitly modeling clause interactions and positive-negative literal relationships.

paragraphs: Aligning diffusion models through reinforcement learning requires connecting the generation process to the quality of its final output. This paper identifies a mismatch in existing approaches, including variants of Direct Preference Optimization: they treat trajectory likelihoods as though they were final-state probabilities. The authors argue that this simplification leads to suboptimal alignment.

Their framework uses the optimal value function as the return for short trajectory segments. First, it learns a value-distribution function to estimate these segment-level returns. Second, an algorithm called VRPO uses those estimates to refine the score function, which guides the diffusion process. This gives intermediate segments a training signal grounded in their value.

Under sufficient model capacity, the authors prove equivalence to training on a reward-tilted distribution proportional to p(x) exp(eta r(x)). This distribution reweights the original probability according to reward. Experiments on large-scale diffusion models show stable, consistent improvements over prior methods. The theoretical result is conditional on model capacity, while the experiments support the framework’s practical alignment benefits.
icml-2026-value-as-return-a-two-stage-fr.tldr: Value-as-Return aligns diffusion models using learned segment values, with a conditional guarantee of matching a reward-tilted target distribution.

paragraphs: Understanding a long video stream requires retaining useful information after earlier content has passed. video-SALMONN S addresses this with a streaming audio-visual language model that processes videos longer than three hours at one frame per second and 360p resolution. The authors report that it outperforms strong non-streaming models under the same memory budget.

Alongside token merging or downsampling, the model uses test-time training to convert short-term multimodal representations into long-term memory stored in model parameters. A dedicated memory layer includes a long-span prediction objective. A two-stage training scheme and a modality-aware memory reader further support long-range dependencies and access to the stored information.

The authors also introduce ELViM, a benchmark in which models must learn from videos observed hours earlier. Across long-video benchmarks, video-SALMONN S improves on streaming and non-streaming baselines by 3–7%. On ELViM, it achieves a 15-percentage-point absolute accuracy improvement over strong non-streaming models. These findings support parameter-based streaming memory for retaining and using earlier audiovisual experience.
icml-2026-video-salmonn-s-memory-enhance.tldr: video-SALMONN S stores streaming audiovisual experience in model parameters, improving long-video understanding and learning from videos seen hours earlier.
